about: The attack index in the Lessons section (docs/sections-plan.md, slice P3). One row for each attack run that the Host registers. The lesson, the expected code and the check name come from GET /api/lessons and /api/lessons/0, so they are not written here. tourStep is the tour step whose try-it plays the run, or null when no tour plays it. guard says what stops the attack, or what would.

runs.guard: The client compares the echo with what it sent, so one changed byte shows. A plain compare finds the change but cannot prove who made it.
Nothing catches this: CBC hides data but carries no tag. Add a MAC over the cipher text, or use GCM, to catch the edit.
The GCM tag covers every locked byte, so the receiver refuses the message when one bit changes.
Never use one GCM nonce twice under one key. A counter or a fresh random nonce per message keeps each one unique.
Nothing catches this: ECB locks equal blocks to equal cipher blocks, so patterns leak. Use a mode with an IV or nonce, such as GCM.
HMAC hashes the inner digest again under the key, so an attacker cannot extend the message and keep a valid seal.
Nothing catches this: a SHA-256 of key plus message can be extended with no key. Use HMAC in its place.
The receiver computes the CMAC again with the shared key, and a changed message gives a different tag.
The receiver computes the CMAC again with the shared key, so a changed tag no longer matches the message.
A plain hash shows that bytes changed, but anyone can compute a new hash. A keyed seal such as HMAC also proves who sent it.
The receiver computes the HMAC again with the shared key, and a changed message gives a different seal.
The receiver computes the HMAC again with the shared key, so a changed seal no longer matches the message.
A changed ML-KEM cipher text gives the two sides different keys, and the key confirmation MAC shows the mismatch.
A swapped share gives the two sides different keys, and the key confirmation MAC shows the mismatch before any data moves.
The client checks the certificate's validity dates against its clock and refuses a certificate outside them.
The issuer's signature covers every byte of the certificate, so one changed byte fails the signature check.
CertificateVerify is a signature over the handshake by the certificate's key. A changed byte fails it, so the server proves it holds the key.
The client follows the chain to a root it already trusts. A chain that ends at any other root is refused.
The client compares the certificate's name with the server name it asked for, and refuses a certificate for another name.
After the handshake, TLS 1.3 accepts only protected records. A clear close_notify in place of data is a message not allowed in that state.
Finished is a MAC over the whole handshake, so a changed byte anywhere in the handshake fails it.
A changed ML-KEM cipher text gives the two sides different keys, so the first protected record fails its AEAD tag.
Each TLS 1.3 record carries an AEAD tag, so the receiver refuses a record with one changed byte.
A longer length makes the receiver wait for bytes that never come. A read deadline ends the wait with a named error.
A replaced key share gives the two sides different keys, so the first protected record fails its AEAD tag.
The reader erases each used DUKPT key, so a past key is no longer in its state, and the reader refuses the request.
The bank decrypts the PIN block and checks its format, so a changed bit gives a block that fails the format check.
The bank records each key serial number it has seen and refuses a sale that reuses one.
A stolen server key opens a recorded RSA session. The same key opens nothing on ECDHE, because neither side stores the private halves of the shares that made its keys.
A TLS 1.3 server that is forced to an older version writes a sentinel into its random value. A client that speaks TLS 1.3 sees it and stops.
Each TLS 1.1 record carries an HMAC, so the receiver refuses a record with one changed byte.
A server that speaks only TLS 1.3 refuses an old client with a protocol_version alert in place of a weak handshake.
The client compares the host key with the one in known_hosts and stops when it changed.
The server signs the exchange hash with its host key, so one changed byte fails the signature check.
Each SSH packet carries a MAC, so the receiver refuses a packet with one changed byte.
The legacy exchange is signed too, so one changed byte fails the exchange signature check.
The server keeps an allow list of tunnel targets and refuses a tunnel to a target that is not on it.
The server checks the user's signature against the user's listed key and refuses a key it does not list.
An X25519 result of all zeros means a bad share. The client checks for it and stops.
The PIN block carries a MAC from the device to the bank, so a bit changed inside the gateway fails at the bank.
The SSH packet MAC on the first hop catches a changed byte before the gateway passes it on.
The TLS 1.3 AEAD tag on the second hop catches a changed byte before the bank reads it.
The issuer signs every token, so a changed claim fails the token signature check.
The server verifies the client certificate and answers a damaged one with a bad_certificate alert.
The server checks the token's expiry time and refuses a token after it.
A server that requires a client certificate answers a client with none with a certificate_required alert.
The issuer accepts each challenge answer once, so an answer sent again is refused.
The server records each DPoP proof's jti, so a proof sent again is refused.
DPoP binds the token to the client's key, so a stolen token used with another key fails the proof binding check.
The server checks each call against what the token grants and refuses a call it does not grant.
The issuer keeps the challenge it sent in this login and refuses an answer to any other challenge.
The issuer accepts a login only from a device key it enrolled, and refuses any other key.
The server checks that the token names it as the audience and refuses a token issued for another server.
The server compares the name in the client certificate with the names it allows and refuses any other name.
The server checks each call against the role in the token and refuses a call that the role does not permit.
A constant-time compare takes the same time whatever the guess, so the timing gives the attacker nothing.
Nothing catches this: a compare that stops at the first wrong byte leaks the answer in its timing. Use a constant-time compare.
